questions.prompt: What percentage of Apex code coverage does Salesforce require org-wide before Apex can be deployed to production?
questions.explain: The Apex Developer Guide requires unit tests to cover at least 75% of Apex code org-wide, with all tests passing, before deployment to production or packaging for the AppExchange.
questions.distractorExplain: 60% sounds like a reasonable 'majority' threshold, but it isn't the number Salesforce actually enforces — the documented floor is specifically 75%, not 60%.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the annotation that marks a class or method as test-only Apex code, excluded from the org's Apex code size limit, is @________.
questions.explain: @isTest is the modern annotation for test classes and test methods; the older 'testMethod' keyword still compiles but is no longer the recommended style.

questions.prompt: A test method inserts an Account, calls AccountService.setDefaultIndustry(), then queries the Account back and checks its Industry field against the expected value. Which three-part structure does this test follow?
options: Assert, Act, Arrange
Arrange, Act, Assert
Act, Assert, Arrange
Assert, Arrange, Act
questions.explain: This is the Arrange/Act/Assert pattern: build the data and inputs (Arrange), call the method under test (Act), then check the result (Assert).

questions.prompt: Match each Assert class method to what it checks.
right: Forces an immediate test failure, often used right after a call expected to throw, to catch the case where it didn't
Fails unless the given condition evaluates to true
Fails unless the value is null
Fails unless the two values are equal
questions.explain: areEqual checks two values match, isNull checks a value is null, isTrue checks a condition is true, and fail() forces an immediate failure — commonly placed right after a call expected to throw, to catch the case where it doesn't.

questions.prompt: A TestDataFactory.createContacts(accountId, count) method accepts a count parameter and returns a list of Contacts. What is the main benefit of this design over a method that always returns exactly one hardcoded Contact?
options: The same factory method can serve both a single-record test and a 200-record bulk test without any changes to the factory
It automatically inserts the records into the database
It removes the need for any assertions in the test
It bypasses the 75% code coverage requirement
questions.explain: A flexible factory accepting a count can build exactly as many records as a given test scenario needs, serving both narrow unit tests and bulk tests from the same method.

questions.prompt: A test class has one @TestSetup method that inserts a shared Account. Test method A updates that Account's Industry field; Test method B runs afterward and queries the same Account. What Industry value does Test method B see?
options: The value Test method A set it to, since changes carry over between methods
The original value from @TestSetup, since per-method changes to setup data are rolled back after that method finishes
Null, since @TestSetup data is deleted after the first test method
Whichever value was set most recently across any test method in the org
questions.explain: Data created in @TestSetup is shared across test methods, but any changes an individual test method makes to it are rolled back once that method finishes — so the next method always sees the original, unmodified setup data.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about @isTest(SeeAllData=true).
options: It gives a test visibility into the org's existing data, bypassing the default test data isolation
It is incompatible with @TestSetup methods in the same class
It is the recommended default approach for every new Apex test
It is discouraged for everyday use because it makes tests less portable across orgs
questions.explain: SeeAllData=true opts a test into seeing real org data and cannot be combined with @TestSetup — it's meant for rare edge cases, not the default approach, since it makes tests depend on org-specific data that may not exist elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What is the term for trigger or handler code written to behave correctly whether it processes 1 record or 200 records in the same transaction?
options: Idempotent
Bulk-safe
Asynchronous
Declarative
questions.explain: Bulk-safe describes code written to work correctly regardless of how many records fire it in a single transaction — the opposite of code with SOQL or DML mistakenly placed inside a loop over Trigger.new.
questions.distractorExplain: Idempotent describes code that produces the same result no matter how many times it runs — a different property from handling varying batch sizes in one transaction, which is what 'bulk-safe' specifically describes.

questions.prompt: A trigger handler issues one SOQL query inside a for loop over Trigger.new. A test inserting a single Account passes. A test inserting 200 Accounts in one DML statement fails with a governor limit exception. Why?
options: With 200 Accounts, the loop issues roughly 200 queries in one transaction, which can exceed the 100-query synchronous SOQL limit; with 1 Account it issues only 1 query, well under the limit
200-record tests always use different, stricter governor limits than 1-record tests
Apex automatically blocks any trigger from processing more than 100 records
The single-record test doesn't actually run the trigger at all
questions.explain: SOQL-in-a-loop issues one query per record — harmless with 1 record, but with 200 records in one transaction it can breach the documented 100-query synchronous limit, which is exactly why bulk tests at a realistic record count matter.

questions.prompt: A test uses System.runAs(salesRep) to query Opportunities as a standard-profile user with no sharing access to a record. Separately, that same user has no field-level-security access to the Amount field, but a plain query inside runAs still returns Amount. Why?
options: System.runAs enforces record sharing but does not by itself enforce object or field-level permissions
System.runAs only works for Account records, not Opportunities
Field-level security is disabled during all Apex tests
The query must have failed to compile
questions.explain: runAs switches the sharing context to the given user, so role hierarchy and sharing rules apply — but it does not by itself enforce field-level or object permissions, which require a separate mechanism such as WITH USER_MODE.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: to fake an HTTP callout's response in an Apex test, you write a class implementing the ________ interface and register it with Test.setMock.
questions.explain: A mock class implements HttpCalloutMock, providing a respond(HttpRequest) method, and is registered with Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, mockInstance) so callouts during the test are intercepted and answered by it.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order for testing a Queueable job that updates Account records.
items: Insert the Account records the job will process
Call System.enqueueJob() with the Queueable instance
Query the Accounts back and assert the job's expected changes
questions.explain: Data is arranged first, then the governor-limit boundary opens with startTest(), the job is enqueued, stopTest() forces it to run synchronously to completion, and only then can the test reliably assert on its effects.

questions.prompt: A negative test calls AccountService.withdraw(acc.Id, 150) inside a try block expecting an InsufficientFundsException, followed immediately by Assert.fail(). If withdraw() does NOT throw at all due to a bug, what happens?
options: Execution reaches Assert.fail(), correctly failing the test since the expected exception never occurred
The test passes, since no exception means no error
The catch block runs anyway and silently passes the test
Apex automatically retries the withdraw() call
questions.explain: Assert.fail() placed right after the call under test is what makes this a valid negative test — if the expected exception doesn't occur, execution reaches Assert.fail() and the test correctly fails instead of passing for the wrong reason.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about positive and negative Apex tests.
options: A positive test proves the code behaves correctly with valid input
A negative test proves the code correctly rejects invalid input or a business rule violation
A method is fully proven correct once only its positive tests pass
Validation rules and addError() calls are common sources of logic that need negative-path testing
questions.explain: Positive and negative tests prove opposite sides of a method's behavior; a method with only positive tests passing is not actually proven correct, since the rejection paths (often validation rules and addError() calls) remain unexercised.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum execution time Salesforce allows for a single Apex transaction?
options: 1 minute
5 minutes
10 minutes
30 minutes
questions.explain: The documented maximum execution time for each Apex transaction is 10 minutes, the same in both synchronous and asynchronous contexts.
questions.distractorExplain: 5 minutes is a plausible-sounding guess but isn't the documented figure — the Apex Developer Guide's Execution Governors and Limits page specifically states 10 minutes as the per-transaction execution cap.

questions.prompt: A test hardcodes an Account Id copied from a sandbox: [SELECT Id FROM Account WHERE Id = '001xx000003DGb2AAG']. What happens when this test runs in a freshly created scratch org?
options: It fails, because that specific record Id does not exist in the new org
It passes identically, since Salesforce Ids are portable across every org
Apex automatically substitutes an equivalent record
It only fails if the scratch org has no licenses available
questions.explain: Salesforce record Ids are not portable across orgs — a hardcoded Id is really a hardcoded dependency on one specific org's data existing at one specific moment, and it fails immediately in any other org.

questions.prompt: Match each documented synchronous Apex governor limit to its value.
questions.explain: Synchronous Apex allows 100 SOQL queries, 150 DML statements, 100 callouts, and 10,000 milliseconds of CPU time per transaction — all documented on the Execution Governors and Limits page.

questions.prompt: A codebase sits at 85% org-wide Apex code coverage, but one previously-passing test now fails after a recent change. Can the team deploy to production?
options: No — all tests must complete successfully, which is a requirement separate from the coverage percentage
Yes, because coverage is well above the 75% floor
Yes, as long as the failing test isn't for a trigger
It depends on whether the failing test uses SeeAllData=true
questions.explain: Coverage and 'all tests passing' are two separate, simultaneous deployment requirements — a single failing test blocks deployment regardless of how high the org-wide coverage percentage is.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails against completely unchanged code is called a ________ test.
questions.explain: A flaky test inconsistently passes or fails against unchanged code, commonly caused by test order-dependence, colliding test data, or an unreliable timing assumption — the correct response is to investigate it like a bug, not just re-run it until it passes.

questions.prompt: A team adds a code-review checklist item requiring every pull request to state its before/after org-wide coverage number, not just 'tests pass.' What problem is this specifically meant to catch?
options: A change that keeps all its own tests passing while still being part of a codebase that could be sitting below the org-wide 75% coverage floor needed to actually deploy
Whether the pull request author used tabs or spaces
Whether the Apex class uses triggers instead of Flow
Whether the test class includes a @TestSetup method
questions.explain: Since Salesforce's 75% requirement is computed org-wide rather than per class, stating the actual coverage number in review surfaces a shortfall that 'all my tests pass' alone would hide.
